\chapter{Who You Give It To}
\label{ch:mr-object-marking}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can mark a person I act on with -lā and leave a thing bare, and I can say that I give or bring something to somebody.}

Complete MR-R47-give-it-to and say three sentences whose -lā does three different jobs: the experiencer who likes, the person seen, and the person given to.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mitrālā]{\mr{मित्राला} (mitrālā) — the object that is a person}

\label{lesson:MR-C47-laa-object}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला}} has been in this book since chapter sixteen, always in front of \emph{liking} or \emph{knowing}. The \textbf{-\mr{ला}} inside it has a second job you have never been shown.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kuṭhūn}, then \emph{udyāpāsūn}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a person you act on takes -\mr{ला}; a thing does not}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मित्राला} \mr{पाहतो}.} — \emph{mī mitrālā pāhto.} — \textbf{I see my friend.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{पाणी} \mr{पाहतो}.} — \emph{mī pāṇī pāhto.} — \textbf{I see water.}
\end{quote}

Read those two across. Same verb, same position, and the marker appears on one and not the other. Marathi puts \textbf{-\mr{ला}} on a direct object when the object is \textbf{animate} — a person, and usually an animal — and leaves it bare when the object is a thing.

If you know Spanish this is the \emph{personal a} under another name, and it behaves the same way: it is not politeness and not emphasis, it is a rule, and dropping it on a person is a mistake rather than a shade.

The stem is the usual one: \textbf{\mr{मित्र} $\to$ \mr{मित्रा}-}, then \textbf{-\mr{ला}}. And now the old \textbf{\mr{मला}} makes sense: it is \textbf{\mr{मी}} through its oblique, with this same \textbf{-\mr{ला}} on the end.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mī mitrālā pāhto} — the friend is marked
  \item \emph{mī pāṇī pāhto} — water is not
  \item \emph{malā} — and hear the same \textbf{-\mr{ला}} you have used since chapter sixteen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which objects take \textbf{-\mr{ला}}? (\textbf{Animate ones} — people and animals.) Is leaving it off a person a shade of meaning or a mistake? (\textbf{A mistake}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mitrālā deto]{\mr{मित्राला} \mr{देतो} (mitrālā deto) — giving it to somebody}

\label{lesson:MR-C47-laa-recipient}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मित्राला} \mr{पाहतो}} marks the person as the one being seen. The same ending marks a different role entirely, and the verb decides which.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the thing stays bare, the person takes -\mr{ला}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मित्राला} \mr{पाणी} \mr{देतो}.} — \emph{mī mitrālā pāṇī deto.} — \textbf{I give water to my friend.}
\end{quote}

Three pieces, and each one is somewhere you can predict. The \textbf{giver} is first and bare. The \textbf{receiver} takes \textbf{-\mr{ला}}. The \textbf{thing given} stays bare because it is not animate. The verb, as always, is last.

English has two ways to say this — \emph{give my friend water}, \emph{give water to my friend} — and has to choose an order. Marathi has one marker and does not care very much about the order of the two objects, because \textbf{-\mr{ला}} already says which is which. That is the payoff of marking rather than positioning.

\textbf{\mr{आणणे}} works the same way: \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मित्राला} \mr{पाणी} \mr{आणतो}}, \emph{I bring water to my friend}. Any verb of handing over takes this frame, and you already have three of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mī mitrālā pāṇī deto}
  \item the same sentence with \emph{āṇto} — I bring it
  \item which of the two objects carries the marker — \textbf{the person}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \emph{I give water to my friend}, which noun takes \textbf{-\mr{ला}}? (\textbf{The friend}.) Why does Marathi not need to fix the order of the two objects? (\textbf{The marker already says which is which}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mitrālā]{One ending, three jobs}

\label{lesson:MR-R47-give-it-to}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{-\mr{ला}} has now appeared in three different sentences doing three different things. Name them before you read on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{malā chahā āvaḍto} — the \textbf{experiencer} carries it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mī mitrālā pāhto} — the \textbf{person acted on} carries it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mī mitrālā pāṇī deto} — the \textbf{receiver} carries it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{ठेवणे}} and put something under the room — \emph{khoolīkhālī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides which of the three jobs \textbf{-\mr{ला}} is doing in a given sentence? (\textbf{The verb}.) Which of the two objects in \emph{I give my friend water} carries it? (\textbf{The friend}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
